analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all federal income tax on profits from selling long-held assets.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have eliminated the federal tax on long-term capital gains retroactively, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have removed 100% of long-term capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, or other property held more than a year — from taxable income. It applied retroactively to sales after December 31, 1994. The bill was introduced by Rep. David Dreier with two Republican cosponsors in January 1996 and was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who realize long-term capital gains — overwhelmingly households in the top income brackets, since most capital gains income goes to them. Someone who sold stock or a business at a profit would pay zero federal income tax on that profit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill excludes 100% of long-term capital gain from gross income, so no federal income tax would be owed on profits from selling property held long-term.
It applies retroactively to sales and exchanges occurring after December 31, 1994, so gains taxpayers had already realized would also become tax-free.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, because the Treasury would collect no income tax on capital gains — a revenue source that flows overwhelmingly from the wealthiest households. Lost revenue would have to be made up through other taxes, future borrowing, or smaller public spending.

drawbacks.text: Because capital gains income is concentrated among the highest-earning households, the tax break's benefits would flow mainly to them while the revenue loss is shared by everyone who pays federal taxes or relies on federal programs.
The retroactive effective date would give a windfall to gains already realized before the bill was introduced, rewarding transactions completed under the old tax rules.
The bill contains no revenue offset, so its entire cost would add to the deficit or require offsetting tax increases elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a complete tax exemption on long-term investment profits, a benefit that accrues mainly to the wealthiest households, with no accompanying revenue offset. Its backers framed it as a spur to investment and job creation — hence the title — but the bill text itself is purely a tax exclusion, and the largest direct gains would go to those with the most realized gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Dreier introduced the bill on January 5, 1996, with Reps. Tauzin and Zimmer joining as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction and received no further action.
The bill would have excluded 100% of long-term capital gains from taxable income, effective retroactively to sales after December 31, 1994.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, capital gains remained taxable and the Treasury kept the revenue it would otherwise have lost; no industry or household received the proposed exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers, since the tax stayed in place

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate tax on long-term capital gains.

for.name: Reps. Tauzin and Zimmer
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair never scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 5, 1996 and took no further action — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Republicans; the bill attracted no Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Investors with large capital gains and the asset-management industry
industries.note: The bill would have made long-term investment profits entirely tax-free, a large benefit concentrated among high-income households and the financial sector that manages their assets. It never passed, so they gained nothing, but if it had, the cost would have fallen on general taxpayers.
